The user's premise contains a factual error: "because it was weather, United only has to give me a travel credit, not my money back." That's wrong under US DOT rules. Actually, weather cancellation = no compensation required, but the passenger is entitled to a refund of the unused ticket if they choose not to travel / if the airline cancels and they don't accept rebooking. DOT rules: if a flight is cancelled and the passenger chooses not to travel, they are entitled to a full refund to original form of payment, regardless of cause, even weather. The "weather" excuse applies to compensation/amenities, not refunds. So the agent is wrong. This is the key fact the user relies on — the ticket was $412.

So the answer: correct the fact, and note that the meeting is today, they drove home. They asked for a message accepting travel credit. I should write the message but also flag that they may prefer a refund of $412 to original payment method, which they're entitled to. Since they said "Fine, I'll take the credit" — I can write the message but include the correction and maybe offer a version requesting refund. The user's own decision is theirs — I should give them the message they asked for, plus note the refund right. Maybe write the message so it works either way, or provide the credit version as asked and mention they can switch.

Time-sensitivity: DOT refund rules — 2024 DOT final rule on refunds requires automatic refunds when airline cancels and passenger doesn't accept alternatives. Effective October 28, 2024. Refund must be to original form of payment, within 7 business days for credit card. Cause doesn't matter for refunds — weather included. "Significant delay" too.

Let me be careful: DOT rule: "When a flight is canceled or significantly delayed, passengers are entitled to a refund if they choose not to travel, regardless of the reason." Yes. Airlines often tell passengers weather = no refund, which is wrong.

Also, the "credit good for at least a year" — DOT rules on travel credits: credits must not expire before 1 year from purchase? Actually there's the 2024 rule that expiration of credits... DOT rule says airlines must not set expiration dates earlier than 12 months from the date of issuance for travel credits? Let me recall: The 2024 final rule requires that flight credits/travel vouchers issued for cancelled flights... Hmm. Actually 49 USC 42304? There's a requirement: travel credits must be valid for at least 5 years? No — that's the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act (May 2024): "air carriers may not set an expiration date earlier than 5 years after the date the credit was issued." Yes! FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Section 501, requires airline travel credits to be valid for at least 5 years from issuance. Hmm, is that correct? I recall the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 included a provision that airlines must accept flight credits for at least 5 years. Let me think... Yes, there was a "flight credits don't expire" provision: airlines required to accept vouchers/credits for at least 5 years after issuance, and to disclose expiration policies. That was in the FAA reauthorization bill signed May 2024.

So asking for "at least a year" undersells — they're legally entitled to 5 years if this is a credit/voucher under that provision. # US Airline Industry Regulatory Updates: Avoiding Thunderheads in New FAA Reauthorization

May 21, 2024

The US aviation industry has been in the headlines recently with the passage of a comprehensive bill to authorize funding of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) for five more years as well as Department of Transportation (DOT) litigation surrounding the Biden administration’s crackdown on what it refers to as “junk fees.” This is on the heels of several other regulatory updates from the first half of 2024.

### FAA REAUTHORIZATION ACT OF 2024: IMPLICATIONS AND IMPLEMENTATION

President Joseph Biden recently signed the landmark [FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024](https://www.commerce.senate.gov/services/files/BC96EBA2-77A1-401C-96A0-E9B990F4D3E4) following overwhelmingly bipartisan support in Congress.

A far-reaching piece of legislation, the act authorizes $105 billion to the FAA and an additional $738 million to the National Transportation Safety Board with a stated aim to address flight delays and cancellations, modernize airport technology, and improve the consumer experience. Provisions relevant to air carriers include the following:

-   **Enhancements for aircraft certification forms:** Building upon the [Aircraft Certification, Safety and Accountability Act of 2020 (ACSAA)](https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/senate-bill/3969/text), the bill adds new oversight and accountability requirements to promote compliance with FAA safety standards for designing and manufacturing aircraft, including requirements around public notice and the opportunity for public comment on significant aircraft design changes.
-   **Codification of automatic refunds:** Sets standards in law for passenger refunds when an airline cancels or significantly delays a flight. Customers will not need to request the refunds and, when airline credits are offered as an option in lieu of a refund to the original form of payment, credits must be valid for five years and convertible to the original form of payment on request within that time period. Furthermore, airlines must establish policies around reimbursement for reasonable costs of care incurred, such as lodging and meals, due to a cancellation or delay.
-   **Fee-free family seating:** Prohibits airlines from charging families with young children to sit together and requires that adjacent seating be provided for parents with young children in most, but not all, circumstances.
-   **Accessibility enhancements:** Strengthens DOT enforcement provisions of the Air Carrier Access Act that makes it illegal for airlines to discriminate against passengers due to a disability. Additionally, the bill requires airline personnel to be trained in safely storing motorized wheelchairs.
-   **Customer Service Requirements:** Airlines must maintain 24/7 live telephone, chat, and text customer service channels free of charge.
-   **Penalties for airline violations:** An accountability measure, the Reauthorization Act triples the DOT’s maximum civil penalty for consumer violations from $25,000 to $75,000, per violation.

Now that the bill is signed into law, we anticipate that airlines will need to act quickly to ensure they comply with the provisions therein. Air carriers should:

-   update their operational procedures;
-   ensure that internal controls and processes, as well as employee training programs, are in compliance with the new law; and
-   confirm the viability of existing customer service infrastructure, including safeguarding against evolving cyberthreats, to ensure 24/7 availability in compliance with Chapter 423 of Title 49 § 42307.

### OPPOSITION TO DOT FEE DISCLOSURE RULES

Several US airlines and an industry trade association recently filed a [suit](https://assets.bwbx.io/documents/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/r0O0yUQQaqoY/v0) in the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit challenging the DOT’s ancillary fee rule that was finalized last month and set to go into effect on July 1. In it, the DOT seeks to require airlines to notify consumers upfront about fees charged for checked and carry-on baggage and reservation changes or cancellations.

This is part of a wider crackdown by the Biden administration, Federal Trade Commission (FTC) rulemaking, and Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) enforcement on so-called “junk fees,” which has brought a number of consumer-oriented sectors into the fray, including airlines, credit card companies, hotels, and live events.

With the lawsuit, airlines are underscoring their position on the fee transparency debate, calling the new rule “an abuse of discretion.” If authorized, airlines will be required to provide upfront disclosure of all fees associated with air travel. The industry had previously scored a win in the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 when Congress was convinced to drop plans to mandate baggage and change fee disclosures.

The airlines have so far not challenged the separate DOT rule requiring automatic cash refunds for canceled flights.

For more information on the crackdown on these fees, refer to our Insights [Mitigating the Risk from ‘Junk Fees’](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2024/02/mitigating-the-risk-from-junk-fees) and [Recent Crackdown on Junk Fees: Federal, State, and Private Actions](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2024/01/recent-crackdown-on-junk-fees-federal-state-and-private-actions).

### STATE ATTORNEY GENERAL INVESTIGATIONS TARGETING AIRLINES

On April 18, the DOT and 18 states agreed to a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) that grants more authority to state attorneys general (AGs) to investigate consumer complaints against airlines. The MOU allows signatory state AGs to investigate unfair or deceptive acts or practices violations; ensure that carriers cooperate with investigations; creates an expedited channel for state AGs to report violations; and grants states access to DOT’s nonpublic consumer complaint database. # 14 CFR § 260.6 - Refunding fare for flights cancelled or significantly delayed or changed by carriers.

-   [CFR](#tab_default_1)

[prev](/cfr/text/14/260.5 "Refunding fees for significantly delayed or lost bags.") | [next](/cfr/text/14/260.7 "Affirmative acceptance of an offer of alternative compensation.")

§ 260.6 Refunding fare for flights cancelled or significantly delayed or changed by carriers.

(a) Carriers' obligation to provide refunds—(1) Carriers' obligation. A [covered carrier](/definitions/index.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=045413330ae7869bec33a0da6cb55935&term_occur=999&term_src=Title:14:Chapter:II:Subchapter:A:Part:260:260.6) that is the [merchant of record](/definitions/index.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=149199e3363842c2206e7dcc6186e01f&term_occur=999&term_src=Title:14:Chapter:II:Subchapter:A:Part:260:260.6) must provide a full and [prompt refund](/definitions/index.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=c58c9e6630c43f35c345f99ae94359b0&term_occur=999&term_src=Title:14:Chapter:II:Subchapter:A:Part:260:260.6) of the airfare, including any taxes and ancillary fees, as set forth in [paragraph (a)(2)](#a_2) of this section to a consumer that holds a nonrefundable ticket on a scheduled flight to, from, or within the United States for any [cancelled flight](/definitions/index.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=7823869a6cc57108e72540cafeb846bf&term_occur=999&term_src=Title:14:Chapter:II:Subchapter:A:Part:260:260.6) or [significantly delayed or changed flight](/definitions/index.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=81474f57e1a7c5d4347737a5af3b0643&term_occur=999&term_src=Title:14:Chapter:II:Subchapter:A:Part:260:260.6) where the consumer chooses not to:

(i) Fly on the significantly delayed or changed flight or accept rebooking on an alternative flight; or

(ii) Accept any voucher, credit, or other form of compensation offered by the [air carrier](/definitions/index.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=96fa7a8f033dbc2683d162f2eccd8889&term_occur=999&term_src=Title:14:Chapter:II:Subchapter:A:Part:260:260.6) or [foreign air carrier](/definitions/index.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=144dc44e291a8bd387236b2c7f6faecf&term_occur=999&term_src=Title:14:Chapter:II:Subchapter:A:Part:260:260.6) pursuant to [paragraph (c)](#c) of this section.

(2) [Automatic refunds](/definitions/index.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=acc03d51e26f28198f42a963f59a4695&term_occur=999&term_src=Title:14:Chapter:II:Subchapter:A:Part:260:260.6). A full refund of the airfare, including any taxes and ancillary fees, is due to a consumer as described in paragraphs (a)(2)(i) through (iii) of this section:

(i) A flight is canceled and a consumer is not offered an alternative flight or any voucher, credit, or other form of compensation by the air carrier or foreign air carrier pursuant to [paragraph (c)](#c) of this section;

(ii) A consumer rejects the significantly delayed or changed flight, rebooking on an alternative flight, or any voucher, credit, or other form of compensation offered by the covered carrier pursuant to [paragraph (c)](#c) of this section; or

(iii) A consumer does not respond to an offer of:

(A) A significantly delayed or changed flight or an alternative flight and the flight departs without the consumer; or

(B) A voucher, credit, or other form of compensation by the date on which the cancelled flight was scheduled to depart or the date that the significantly delayed or changed flight departs.

(b) Individuals with a disability. A carrier that is the merchant of record must provide a full and prompt refund to an [individual with a disability](/definitions/index.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=d9b0b07384ce9e309469a9a2005a40a6&term_occur=999&term_src=Title:14:Chapter:II:Subchapter:A:Part:260:260.6) upon notification by the individual with a disability that he/she does not want to continue travel because of the significant changes described in paragraphs (b)(1) through (3) of this section. The covered carrier must also provide a full and prompt refund to any individuals in the same reservation as the individual with a disability who do not want to continue travel without the individual with a disability in situations described in paragraphs (b)(1) through (3).

(1) The individual with a disability is downgraded to a lower [class of service](/definitions/index.php?width=840&height=800&iframe=true&def_id=5930901c8e851a0cb0272406ebd0955e&term_occur=999&term_src=Title:14:Chapter:II:Subchapter:A:Part:260:260.6) that results in one or more accessibility features needed by the individual becoming unavailable.

(2) The individual with a disability is scheduled to travel through one or more connecting airports that are different from the original itinerary.

(3) The individual with a disability is scheduled to travel on a substitute aircraft on which one or more accessibility features available on the original aircraft needed by the individual are unavailable.

(c) Alternative to refund. A covered carrier may offer a voucher, credit, or other form of compensation as an explicit alternative to providing a refund required by [paragraph (a)](#a) of this section if:

(1) The offer includes a clear and conspicuous notice of—

(i) The terms of the offer as specified in [§ 260.8](/cfr/text/14/260.8); and

(ii) The consumer's right to a full refund under this section.

(3) Upon the issuance of such voucher, credit, or other form of compensation, a covered carrier notifies the recipient of the expiration date of the voucher, credit, or other form of compensation; and

**The agent gave you the wrong rule, and it costs you $412 if you take the credit.** Weather excuses a lot for an airline — hotels, meals, rebooking — but not this. Under [14 CFR 260.6(a)(1)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/260.6), when a flight is cancelled and you decline the rebooking, you're entitled to a full refund of the fare to your original form of payment, nonrefundable ticket and weather included. You declined it in effect: the meeting was that day and you drove home. And a credit offered *instead of* that refund must be valid at least five years, not one ([§260.6(c)(2)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/260.6)) — so "at least a year" is asking for less than you already have. If you want the cash, use the second message; if you'd rather have the credit anyway, the first one is what you asked for.
